meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What the hell has Hoover got to do with it? Anyway, I had a better year than he did'?
meta.ogDescription: No 1930 newspaper carries the line. It first appears in a 1947 Babe Ruth biography — and Ruth’s documented answer that January was different.

answer.label: Not Ruth’s documented words — a 1947 retelling
answer.sourceLine: Ruth really did answer the Hoover-salary jab — but not in these words. The famous line has no known contemporary source: its earliest documented appearance is Tom Meany’s 1947 biography Babe Ruth: The Big Moments of the Big Fellow, page 139, where it reads “What the hell has Hoover got to do with this?” Wikiquote calls the version now circulated “likely apocryphal,” while Quote Investigator judges that Ruth probably said something of this type.
answer.confidenceText: Ruth’s idea, but the wording is a sportswriter’s retelling first printed in 1947 — no 1930-era source carries it.

source.excerpt: “What the hell has Hoover got to do with this?” demanded the Babe. “Anyway, I had a better year than he did.”
trail: 7 January 1930 — Ruth, asked what made him think he was worth more than the President, answers on the record about his home-run season and contract length; reported by Richards Vidmer in the New York Herald Tribune the next day, per Wikiquote ↗.

1947 — the familiar wording appears in Tom Meany’s Babe Ruth: The Big Moments of the Big Fellow, p. 139 — the earliest appearance located by Quote Investigator ↗, which notes the episode itself probably occurred circa 1932.
16 December 1947 — Arthur Daley retells the exchange in his New York Times column, dropping the profanity (“What has Hoover got to do with this?”), per Quote Investigator ↗.
26 February 1948 — the Richmond (VA) Times-Dispatch prints the line in Chauncey Durden’s “The Sportview” column, crediting Meany’s book; this is the earliest press citation logged by Barry Popik ↗.

Today — even the National Archives’ Hoover Library blog ↗, which calls these anecdotes a “mythic retelling,” prints the quip in yet another wording: “What the hell does Hoover have to do with it? Besides I had a better year than he did.”
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator from Meany’s 1947 biography, page 139. Note “this,” not the “it” of the modern standard version.

author.name: Babe Ruth
author.heading: About Babe Ruth
author.metaLine: 1895–1948 · American baseball player, New York Yankees
author.bio: George Herman “Babe” Ruth was the defining slugger of baseball’s live-ball era and, by 1930, its highest-paid player. His salary negotiations were front-page news precisely because his pay outran the President’s during an economic collapse — which is why the Hoover comeback, in whatever form he actually delivered it, stuck. Ruth did field the “more than the President” question on the record in January 1930; the polished one-liner people quote today surfaced only after his playing days, in a 1947 biography.

misattribution.heading: How a paraphrase became a quotation
misattribution.intro: Nobody stole this line from another speaker — the drift is subtler. A real exchange was retold from memory years later, then re-polished by columnists until it acquired the crispness of a transcript it never had.

items.why: Meany’s biography renders it “‘What the hell has Hoover got to do with this?’ demanded the Babe. ‘Anyway, I had a better year than he did.’” Today’s standard version swaps in “it.” Quote Investigator ↗ identifies this 1947 page as the earliest appearance it located.

Daley retold it in 1947 without the profanity, then in an August 1948 column moved the episode to 1930 and rephrased it again — even though contemporary newspaper records point to a disagreement circa 1932, per Quote Investigator ↗.

Rogers was already joking in his syndicated column about Ruth being offered the same salary as Hoover — but his punchline was that Ruth “can’t appoint a commission to go up and knock the home runs,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

“Hey, I had a better year than he did,” “Why not, I had a better year than he did” and “I know, but I had a better year than Hoover” all circulate without sources; Barry Popik ↗ logs them alongside the 26 February 1948 Richmond Times-Dispatch printing.

misattribution.truthLine: What Ruth is actually on record saying, when asked on 7 January 1930 why he was worth more than the President: that he’d have broken the home-run record if he hadn’t been sick, and that “the President gets a four-year contract. I’m only asking for three” — reported by Richards Vidmer in the New York Herald Tribune, 8 January 1930, as cited by Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why the line refuses to die
lead: The story only works because the underlying fact is true: in March 1930 newspapers reported Ruth settling for $80,000 a season on a two-year deal — the Dallas Morning News carried it on 9 March 1930, per Barry Popik’s citation file ↗ — more than the President of the United States earned while the country slid into the Depression. A ballplayer out-earning Herbert Hoover was a genuine national talking point, not a joke invented later.

So the retort had somewhere to land. Will Rogers was already working the same material in January 1930 — his syndicated column ran a Ruth-versus-Hoover salary gag with an entirely different punchline. The version everyone repeats today, with its perfect two-beat structure, first shows up in print in 1947, told by a sportswriter who had covered Ruth for years.
context.detailsSummary: What Ruth is actually on record saying
detailsBody: Asked on 7 January 1930 what made him think he was worth more than the President of the United States, Ruth’s reported answer was about his home-run season and his contract length, not a one-line put-down of Hoover’s job performance. Wikiquote cites the exchange to Richards Vidmer’s report in the New York Herald Tribune of 8 January 1930.

Quote Investigator adds a wrinkle the popular version smooths over: contemporary newspaper records suggest the salary disagreement being described probably occurred circa 1932, while columnist Arthur Daley moved it to 1930 in an August 1948 column. The anecdote’s date is as unstable as its wording.
context.pull: The fact is documented. The sentence is not.
